prompt: What is a Spot virtual machine, compared with a regular one of the same size?
hint: Same images, same hardware, same disks.

choices.text: A smaller share of a host, with fewer guaranteed vCPUs than the size promises
choices.why: That is closer to lesson 1's B family. A Spot machine has every vCPU of its size, for as long as it runs.

choices.text: The same machine on capacity Azure is not using, with no priority to keep it
choices.why: Right. Images, hardware, disks and performance are the same; what differs is that Azure takes the capacity back when a regular machine needs it.

choices.text: A machine on older hardware that Azure is retiring, sold off cheaply
choices.why: Microsoft's guide says Spot runs on the same hardware as regular machines. What is cheap is the priority, not the equipment.

choices.text: A regular machine with a 99% SLA instead of the higher one
choices.why: There is no SLA for Spot at all, at any percentage.

prompt: The shop wants to save money on its staging server, a `Standard_B2s_v2`, by declaring it with `priority: 'Spot'`. What does the documentation say about that?
hint: Look at the list of restrictions.

choices.text: It works, and a burstable size gets the largest discount
choices.why: The B-series is the one family the Spot pages name as unsupported.

choices.text: It works, but the credits stop accruing while the machine is Spot
choices.why: The documentation describes no such rule, because the question never arises: B sizes cannot be Spot.

choices.text: It is refused only in `brazilsouth`, where Spot is not offered
choices.why: Spot is offered in every region except Azure operated by 21Vianet; the size is what rules it out.

choices.text: It is not possible: B-series sizes are not supported for Spot
choices.why: Right. B-series and promo sizes are excluded, so the staging server would need a D size to be Spot.

prompt: `priority: 'spot'`, in lower case, compiled with no warning. What does that silence tell you?
hint: The compiler printed the type of `priority` when it was given a number.

choices.text: That Azure accepts the lower-case spelling, since the compiler checks values against Azure's types
choices.why: It checks against the type it has, and for `priority` that type is any string. It compared the value with nothing.

choices.text: Nothing about Azure: its type for `priority` is any string, so there was no list to check
choices.why: Right. Whether Resource Manager takes `spot` is decided by the compute service; copy `Spot` from the CLI's list.

choices.text: That the compiler corrected the case, as the template shows `Spot`
choices.why: The template showed `"spot"`, exactly as written. The compiler changes nothing.

choices.text: That the warning is printed only at deployment, when the subscription is known
choices.why: The compiler warns at build time or not at all; it printed a warning for the number in the same place.

prompt: At an illustrative regular rate of 0.20 USD an hour, and supposing for the arithmetic a Spot discount of 60%, what do 300 Spot hours cost, in USD?
hint: You pay 40% of the regular rate.

prompt: The shop's report machine already exists as a regular machine. Somebody adds `priority: 'Spot'` to its file and deploys it again. What should they expect?
hint: When is Spot decided?

choices.text: The machine is converted at its next restart, and billed as Spot from then on
choices.why: The documentation's FAQ says setting Spot is supported only at creation; an existing machine is not converted.

choices.text: A refusal: Spot is set only at creation, so this needs a new machine
choices.why: Right. The error list even has a code for a priority applied to a machine created without one, `VMPriorityCannotBeApplied`.

choices.text: A Spot machine beside the regular one, with the same name and a suffix
choices.why: A deployment never invents a second machine with a new name; it updates the one it names.

choices.text: Nothing, because priority is read only by the CLI and not by Bicep
choices.why: The template carried `"priority": "Spot"`; Resource Manager reads it like any other property.

prompt: What does `maxPrice: -1` decide for a Spot machine?
hint: The portal calls it an eviction type.

choices.text: That the machine is evicted only for capacity, and never billed above the standard price
choices.why: Right. Price is no longer a reason to evict it, and the documentation says you pay the Spot price or the standard one, whichever is lower.

choices.text: That it is never evicted, at the cost of paying the standard price
choices.why: Capacity can always take a Spot machine; -1 removes only the price reason.

choices.text: That there is no maximum, so the hourly price may rise above the standard price
choices.why: The documentation is explicit that you are never charged above the standard price.

choices.text: That the maximum is chosen by Azure each hour from the current price
choices.why: Nobody chooses a maximum; -1 means there is none for eviction purposes.

prompt: Match each part of the machine to what an eviction leaves of it, under each policy.
hint: One policy keeps the machine; the other keeps nothing.

pairs.right: Still counted against the Spot quota
Created by something outside, of any size, in any zone

right_distractors: Restarted by Azure as soon as capacity returns

prompt: `maxPrice: 0.05` made the compiler print five errors and write no template. What is the way to write that maximum in Bicep?
hint: Bicep has integers only.

choices.text: `maxPrice: '0.05'`, as text, which Resource Manager converts
choices.why: Text is what the warning refused for `'-1'`: the type wants a number.

choices.text: `maxPrice: 5`, since the property is in cents
choices.why: The maximum is in US dollars an hour; 5 would be five dollars.

choices.text: `maxPrice: json('0.05')`, which becomes the number 0.05 at deployment
choices.why: Right. It compiled with no warning, and the template carries `[json('0.05')]` for Resource Manager to evaluate.

choices.text: `maxPrice: 0,05`, with the comma Bicep uses for decimals
choices.why: Bicep has no decimal numbers in either notation; a comma separates items.

prompt: A Spot machine with a maximum of 0.04 USD an hour was evicted when the Spot price rose to 0.05. The next day the price is 0.03. What happens to the machine?
hint: Look at the last rows of the documentation's table.

choices.text: It restarts on its own, since the price is under its maximum again
choices.why: The documentation says the machine is not restarted automatically after a price eviction.

choices.text: It restarts on its own, but is billed at its maximum of 0.04
choices.why: Nothing restarts it, and you never pay your maximum, only the current price.

choices.text: It stays stopped until somebody starts it, and is then billed at the current price
choices.why: Right. A price eviction is not undone when the price falls; restarting is yours to do.

choices.text: It is deleted, because a price eviction ignores the eviction policy
choices.why: The eviction policy decides what is left whatever the reason for the eviction.

prompt: Which of these are true of a Spot machine evicted with `Deallocate`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what is still there, and who pays for it.

choices.text: Its disks are kept and billed while it waits
choices.why: The documentation says the storage of the underlying disks is still charged.

choices.text: Its cores still count against the subscription's quota
choices.why: Deallocated machines count against quota, which can block their own replacements.

choices.text: A restart is not guaranteed to succeed
choices.why: Capacity returns when it returns; the documentation says there is no guarantee the allocation will succeed.

choices.text: It may be restarted in another zone where there is room
choices.why: A deallocated machine stays in its region and zone; moving is what Delete and a new machine give you.

choices.text: Azure restarts it on its own when capacity returns
choices.why: Nothing restarts it; something you build has to keep trying, or a scale set's try and restore for instances in a set.

prompt: In the Scheduled Events document, the event type that announces a Spot eviction is ___.
hint: Its minimum notice is 30 seconds.

prompt: Put the report machine's listener in order, from boot to eviction.
hint: It asks long before anything happens.
items: Ask the Scheduled Events endpoint at boot, and every second after
See a new DocumentIncarnation holding a Preempt that names this machine
Send SIGTERM, so the report writes a checkpoint and exits
POST a StartRequests body naming the event
Azure evicts the machine, at NotBefore or sooner
trap: Waiting to start the listener until trouble is suspected: the first answer can take two minutes.

prompt: Why does the listener start at boot, rather than when the machine's metrics suggest an eviction is coming?
hint: What switches Scheduled Events on?

choices.text: Because Azure sends the Preempt only to listeners that registered at boot
choices.why: Nothing registers. The machine asks, and the service answers whoever asks with the header.

choices.text: Its first request switches it on, and that answer takes up to two minutes
choices.why: Right. Thirty seconds of notice are no use to a listener whose first answer is still on its way.

choices.text: Because the metrics are in Azure Monitor, which a machine cannot read
choices.why: There are no metrics that predict an eviction; that is not why the listener starts early.

choices.text: Because a listener started later uses an older api-version
choices.why: The version is whatever the request names, at any time.

prompt: The listener crashes before it acknowledges a Preempt. What happens to the eviction?
hint: What does an acknowledgement change?

choices.text: It is postponed until the machine acknowledges, however long that takes
choices.why: An event does not wait for consent; the documentation says it goes ahead at NotBefore.

choices.text: It is cancelled, and a new Preempt is sent a minute later
choices.why: Nothing cancels an eviction because the machine stayed silent.

choices.text: It becomes a Delete, whatever the policy says
choices.why: The eviction policy is fixed on the machine; the listener has no part in it.

choices.text: It goes ahead at NotBefore, as it would have anyway
choices.why: Right. Acknowledging only lets Azure go ahead sooner; silence never makes the window longer.

prompt: A listener on every instance of a scale set drains its worker on any Preempt it sees, without reading `Resources`. One Spot instance is being evicted. What goes wrong?
hint: Who receives the events of a placement group?

choices.text: Nothing: each instance receives only its own events
choices.why: The documentation says the events of every machine in a scale set placement group are delivered to all of them.

choices.text: All of them stop their workers, while only one machine is leaving
choices.why: Right. The fix is the check `spot-watch.py` makes: act only when this machine's name is in `Resources`.

choices.text: The evicted instance never sees its own event, because another acknowledged it first
choices.why: Every instance can read the event; acknowledgement does not hide it.

choices.text: The scale set refuses the acknowledgements and the eviction is delayed
choices.why: The service answers 200 to any valid event id, even one already acknowledged.

prompt: A Flexible scale set has `baseRegularPriorityCount: 2` and `regularPriorityPercentageAboveBase: 25`. At a capacity of 12, how many of its instances are Spot, rounding as the documentation's examples do?
hint: Take off the base, split the rest, and round the regular share down.

prompt: `orchestrationMode: 'Uniform'` beside a `priorityMixPolicy` compiled with no warning. What should you conclude?
hint: What does the compiler check, and what does it not?

choices.text: That Uniform scale sets now support the mix, since the type lets a Uniform set carry one
choices.why: The documentation says plainly that the mix works only with Flexible; the type knows nothing of that rule.

choices.text: Nothing in its favour: the compiler checks each property alone, and the mix needs Flexible
choices.why: Right. Rules that tie properties together are in the documentation and in Azure's answer to a deployment.

choices.text: That the mix will be applied after the set is converted to Flexible
choices.why: The orchestration mode is chosen once, when the set is created, as lesson 4 said.

choices.text: That a warning appears once a single placement group is set
choices.why: No warning depends on it; the compiler did not compare the two properties at all.

prompt: Lesson 4's autoscale setting is pointed at the shop's Spot workers, which have try and restore enabled. What happens to try and restore?
hint: Who owns the count?

choices.text: It restores evicted instances first, and autoscale adds any still missing
choices.why: The two do not share the count; the documentation says one switches the other off.

choices.text: It stays on, but only for instances evicted for price
choices.why: It only ever restores instances evicted for capacity, and here it is off altogether.

choices.text: It is disabled: the count is now driven by the autoscale rules
choices.why: Right. And the documentation advises Delete for an autoscaled Spot set, so evicted instances do not hold disks and quota.

choices.text: It raises the autoscale minimum to the restored count
choices.why: Nothing changes the autoscale profile; that stays as lesson 4 wrote it.

prompt: The order API needs three machines to answer at all and runs on up to twelve at the busiest hour. How should it use Spot?
hint: What is the minimum for?

choices.text: Not at all, because a production API is too important for Spot
choices.why: Importance is not the test; what one eviction costs is, and above the minimum it costs little.

choices.text: All twelve on Spot, spread over three zones so one eviction takes few
choices.why: Spot evictions can take many at once, and then the API stops answering; the minimum must be regular.

choices.text: A base of three regular machines, and Spot only above it
choices.why: Right. A priority mix with `baseRegularPriorityCount: 3` keeps the API answering on the night every Spot instance goes.

choices.text: Three Spot machines with `maxPrice: -1`, which are never evicted
choices.why: `-1` removes only the price reason; capacity can still take every one of them.

prompt: At an illustrative eviction rate of 20% an hour, what is the chance, in percent, that a three-hour job on one Spot machine finishes with no eviction at all?
hint: Each hour passes with no eviction 80% of the time.

prompt: The nightly report has no checkpoints and must be ready by 07:00. On Spot it saves money every month and misses the deadline on about one night in six. Which change makes Spot safe for it?
hint: What does an eviction throw away?

choices.text: Setting `maxPrice: -1`, so the report is never evicted
choices.why: `-1` removes the price reason only; capacity evictions, the ones in the arithmetic, remain.

choices.text: Writing a checkpoint to Blob Storage every half hour, and one more on SIGTERM
choices.why: Right. An eviction then costs about 25 minutes instead of a restart from nothing, and the deadline holds.

choices.text: Switching the eviction policy to Delete, so the replacement starts faster
choices.why: A faster restart does not bring back two hours of lost work.

choices.text: Polling Scheduled Events ten times a second to get more notice
choices.why: The notice is at most thirty seconds however often you ask, and the service limits a machine to five requests a second.

prompt: In the portal, somebody chose the eviction type *Price or capacity* with a maximum of 0.06 USD an hour. How is that choice written in a Bicep file?
hint: The API has no property named after the portal's choice.

choices.text: `evictionType: 'PriceOrCapacity'` beside `evictionPolicy`
choices.why: The compiler refused `evictionType`: it is not a property of a virtual machine.

choices.text: `evictionPolicy: 'Price'`, with the maximum written in `billingProfile` below it
choices.why: The policy is Deallocate or Delete, what is left afterwards, not the reason for the eviction.

choices.text: `priority: 'Spot'` alone, since an eviction for price is what a Spot machine does by default
choices.why: Capacity is the only reason that is always present; price exists only with a maximum.

choices.text: `billingProfile: { maxPrice: json('0.06') }`, a number instead of -1
choices.why: Right. The eviction type is the value of `maxPrice`, and a decimal needs `json` in Bicep.

prompt: A team wants each Spot worker in a scale set to have several minutes to drain before it is taken away. What notice does the documentation offer?
hint: Look at the minimum notice of each event type, and at what a Spot instance may enable.

choices.text: A Terminate notification of 5 to 15 minutes, set once on the scale set's model
choices.why: Terminate notifications exist for scale set instances, and the documentation says they cannot be enabled on Spot ones.

choices.text: A Redeploy event with ten minutes' notice before each eviction
choices.why: Redeploy is a move to another host, not an eviction; a Spot eviction is a Preempt.

choices.text: At most thirty seconds, through the Preempt event, on a best-effort basis
choices.why: Right. Nothing lengthens it, so the workers must be safe to stop within that time or without any notice.

choices.text: Unlimited time, for as long as the machine has not yet acknowledged the event
choices.why: The event goes ahead at NotBefore whether or not the machine has acknowledged it.

prompt: Ten Spot `D2s_v5` workers, outside any scale set, were evicted with `Deallocate`. The automation that creates replacements now fails, and the illustrative Spot quota is 20 vCPUs. Why, and what would have avoided it?
hint: What do deallocated machines still hold?

choices.text: Their 20 vCPUs are still counted against the quota; `Delete` would have released them
choices.why: Right. Deallocated machines count against quota, so replacements cannot be created until the old ones go or restart.

choices.text: The Spot price rose; `maxPrice: -1` would have avoided it
choices.why: A price above the maximum stops a creation with its own error, and these machines had no maximum problem to begin with.

choices.text: The region has no Spot quota at all; a request for regular quota fixes it
choices.why: The quota was there and in use; Spot quota is a separate pool, raised through the ordinary request.

choices.text: The names are taken; a scale set would have generated new ones
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation ties this failure to names; the deallocated machines are holding the cores.
